'''Rashad Khalifa''' ({{langx|ar|رشاد خليفة}}; November 19, 1935 – January 31, 1990)<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Greenewald |first=John Jr. |date=December 30, 2016 |title=Khalifa, Rashad {{!}} Freedom of Information Act (United States) {{!}} FBI files |url=https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/fbifiles/scientists/rashadkhalifa-fbi1.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250110170548/https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/fbifiles/scientists/rashadkhalifa-fbi1.pdf |archive-date=January 10, 2025 |access-date=November 9, 2025 |website=www.theblackvault.com}}</ref> was an [[Egyptian American|Egyptian-American]] [[biochemist]], closely associated with the [[United Submitters International]] (USI), an organization that promotes the practice and study of "Quran, the Whole Quran, and Nothing But the Quran." Khalifa saw his role as purging the accretions that found their way into Islam via [[hadith]] and [[sunnah]], which he claimed were corruptions. Similarly, he believed that [[Islamic holy books|previous revelations]] of God, such as the [[Bible]], contained contradictions due to human interference<ref name="MasjidSubmission">{{cite web | url=https://www.masjidtucson.org/publications/videos/ | title=Videos: Submission, Rashad Khalifa }}</ref> (a concept known as ''[[tahrif]])''.
Instead, he believed that the beliefs and practices of Islam should be based on the Quran alone. He is also known for his claims regarding the existence of a [[Quran code]], also known as The Number 19. In the last years of his life, Khalifa used the English words “Submission” and “Submitter” instead of the Arabic words ‘Islam’ and “Muslim”, and stated this in his publications and used it in his 1989 translation of the Qur'an.[https://www.masjidtucson.org/publications/books/sp/1989/sep/page1.html] 

His changing views regarding the essence of faith, recorded in his two renditions of the Quran, and declaring himself as a divine messenger who communicated with [[Gabriel (angel)|Gabriel]], drew opposition from other Muslims.<ref name="IslamAwareness">[https://www.islamawareness.net/Deviant/Submitters/rashad_khalifa_purifier_or_pretender.html Rashad Khalifa Purifier or Pretender?], Islamicawareness.net, Accessed January 25, 2020</ref> On January 31, 1990, Khalifa was found stabbed to death inside the Mosque of Tucson, in Arizona, which he founded.<ref name="Calgary police nab suspect" /><ref name=":0" />

==Life==

Khalifa was born in Egypt on November 19, 1935.<ref name=":1" /> He obtained an honors degree from [[Ain Shams University]], before he immigrated to the United States in 1959. He later earned a [[Master's Degree]] in [[biochemistry]] from [[University of Arizona]] and a Ph.D. from [[University of California, Riverside]].<ref name="RK.life">{{Cite web|url=https://www.masjidtucson.org/submission/faq/rashad_khalifa_summary.html|title=Submission (Islam): Rashad Khalifa (Messenger of the Covenant), summary and facts|website=www.masjidtucson.org|access-date=2016-09-09}}</ref> He became a [[Naturalization|naturalized]] U.S. citizen and lived in [[Tucson, Arizona]].<ref name="RK.life"/> He was married to an American woman and they had a son and a daughter together.

Khalifa worked as a science adviser for the Libyan government for about one year, after which he worked as a chemist for the [[United Nations Industrial Development Organization]]. He next worked as a senior chemist in Arizona's State Office of Chemistry in 1980.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/RashadKhalifa|title=Rashad Khalifa|last=Federal Bureau of Investigation}}</ref>

He founded the United Submitters International (USI), an organization that promulgated his beliefs.<ref>{{cite journal
|title=Why the name change
|author=Rashad Khalifa
|date=September 1989
|journal=Submission Perspective
|volume=57
|page=1
|url=http://www.quranalone.com/SP/57_1989_09.pdf
|archive-date=2021-07-31
|access-date=2009-07-26
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210731115713/https://www.quranalone.com/SP/57_1989_09.pdf
|url-status=dead
}}</ref>

==Doctrine==
He saw his role as purging the accretions that found their way into Islam via [[hadith]] and [[sunnah]], which he claimed were corrupted.<ref name="Haddad">Yvonne Yazbeck Haddad and Jane I. Smith, ''Mission to America: five Islamic sectarian communities in North America'', University Press of Florida, 1993, pp. 153 and 160</ref> Similarly, he believed that [[Islamic holy books|previous revelations]] of God, such as the [[Bible]], contained contradictions due to human interference<ref name="MasjidSubmission"/> (a concept known as ''[[tahrif]])''. Instead, he believed that the beliefs and practices of Islam should be based on the [[Quran]] alone.<ref>Aisha Y. Musa, ''Hadith As Scripture: Discussions on the Authority of Prophetic Traditions in Islam'', Palgrave Macmillan, 2008, pp. 87-92</ref>

Starting in 1968, Khalifa used computers to analyze the frequency of letters and words in the Quran. He published his findings in 1973 in the book ''Miracle of the Quran: Significance of the Mysterious Alphabets'', in 1981 in the book ''The Computer Speaks: God's Message to the World'', and in 1982 in the book ''Quran: Visual Presentation of the Miracle''.<ref>Yvonne Yazbeck Haddad and Jane I. Smith, ''Mission to America: five Islamic sectarian communities in North America'', pp. 141-142</ref> Khalifa claimed that the [[Quran]], unlike the [[hadiths|Hadith]], was incorruptible because it contained a mathematical structure based on the number 19, namely the [[Quran code]] or known as Code 19. For example, he claimed that this mathematical structure rejected the Quranic verses 9:128-129.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://submission.org/two_false_verses_deeper_look.html|title=Two False verses; A Deeper Look {{!}} Submission.org - Your best source for Submission (Islam)|website=submission.org|language=en|access-date=2018-11-04}}</ref> Most Muslims object to this interpretation.<ref name="Haddad" /><ref name="IslamAwareness"/> However, Khalifa believed this mathematical structure prevented the Quran from being adulterated and that it was proof of its divine authorship.<ref>[https://19.org/blog/letter-to-signs-magazine/ Letter to Signs Magazine], 19.org, Accessed January 25, 2020</ref>

Khalifa's research did not receive much attention in the [[Western world|West]]. In 1980, [[Martin Gardner]] mentioned it in ''[[Scientific American]]''.<ref>Gardner, Martin (1980), Mathematical Games, ''Scientific American'', September 1980, pp. 16–20.</ref> Gardner later wrote a more extensive and critical review of Khalifa and his work.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://skepticalinquirer.org/1997/09/the_numerology_of_dr_rashad_khalifa/ |url-access=subscription |title=The numerology of Dr. Rashad Khalifa |first=Martin |last=Gardner |journal=Skeptical Inquirer |date=September–October 1997}}</ref>

==Assassination==
On January 31, 1990, Khalifa was found stabbed to death inside the [[mosque]] of [[Tucson, Arizona]], which he founded.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Star |first=Kim Smith, Arizona Daily |date=2012-12-19 |title=Man convicted in 1990 killing of teacher at Tucson mosque |url=https://tucson.com/news/local/crime/article_a5762294-4a36-11e2-a31f-0019bb2963f4.html |access-date=2025-08-31 |website=Arizona Daily Star |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Submission (Islam): Rashad Khalifa (Messenger of the Covenant), summary and facts |url=https://www.masjidtucson.org/submission/faq/rashad_khalifa_summary.html |access-date=2025-08-31 |website=www.masjidtucson.org}}</ref> 

Nineteen years after the murder, on April 28, 2009, the [[Calgary Police Service]] arrested [[Glen Cusford Francis]], a 52-year-old citizen of [[Trinidad and Tobago]], on suspicion of having killed Rashad Khalifa.<ref name="Calgary police nab suspect">{{cite news|url=https://nationalpost.com/related/topics/story.html?id=1547368|title=Calgary police nab suspect in imam killing|last=Massinon|first=Stephane |date=April 30, 2009|work=National Post|publisher=The National Post Company|access-date=2009-05-23}}{{dead link|date=October 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} </ref> Investigators in Tucson learned that Francis, who was going by the name Benjamin Phillips, had begun his studies under Khalifa in January 1990. Phillips disappeared shortly after the slaying,<ref name="Calgary police nab suspect" /> and was said to have left the country. An investigation revealed Phillips and Francis were the same man when the police analyzed [[fingerprints]] found in Phillips' apartment. A specialty unit of the Tucson Police Department progressed in its investigation in 2006 and in December 2008, and was able to use [[DNA testing]] on [[forensic evidence]] from the crime scene to tie Francis to the assassination.<ref name="Fugitive denied bail">{{cite news|url=https://vancouversun.com/Life/Fugitive+held+slaying+American+imam+denied+bail/1621967/story.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090614091749/http://www.vancouversun.com/Life/Fugitive+held+slaying+American+imam+denied+bail/1621967/story.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 14, 2009|title=Fugitive held in slaying of American imam denied bail|last=Slade|first=Daryl|date=May 22, 2009|work=The Vancouver Sun|publisher=Canwest Publishing Inc.|access-date=2009-05-23}}</ref> In October 2009, a Canadian judge ordered Francis's [[extradition]] to the United States to face trial.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://cnews.canoe.com/CNEWS/Crime/2009/10/17/11434296-sun.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160106045513/http://cnews.canoe.com/CNEWS/Crime/2009/10/17/11434296-sun.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 6, 2016|title=Calgary suspect closer to trial for U.S. murder|work=The Calgary Sun|last=Martin|first=Kevin|publisher=Sun Media|access-date=2010-03-18}}</ref>

The trial for the murder began on December 11, 2012. On December 19, the jury, after a three-hour deliberation, found Glen Francis guilty of first-degree murder and sentenced him to life in prison.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://calgaryherald.com/news/Calgarian+faces+life+sentence+1990+murder+controversial/7743101/story.html |title=Calgarian faces life sentence for 1990 murder of controversial U.S. imam |work=Calgary Herald |last=Komarnicki |first=Jamie |publisher=Postmedia Network |access-date=2012-12-28 |archive-date=2012-12-28 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121228235110/http://www.calgaryherald.com/news/Calgarian+faces+life+sentence+1990+murder+controversial/7743101/story.html }}</ref> Prior to the Francis trial, James Williams, an alleged member of the [[Jamaat ul-Fuqra]] organization, was convicted of [[Conspiracy (criminal)|conspiracy]] in the slaying.<ref name=":0">Eric Anderson, "Slain Islamic leader was outspoken; Khalifa's teachings from Tucson angered Muslims worldwide", ''[[Denver Post]]'', 21 October 1993, p21.</ref> Williams disappeared in 1994 on the day of his sentencing.<ref>{{cite news|title=Extremist is 'not to be found'; Little hope held of finding Fuqra fugitive|work=The Rocky Mountain News|access-date=9 September 2026|date=25 February 1994|url=https://www.coloradohistoricnewspapers.org/?a=d&d=RMD19940225-01.2.51}}</ref> In 2000, Williams was apprehended attempting to re-enter the United States and was sentenced to serve 69 years in prison. In 2003, his convictions were upheld on appeal by the [[Colorado Court of Appeals]], except for one count of [[forgery]].<ref>''People v. James D. Williams'', (Colo. App. 01CA0781, Aug. 7, 2003) (not selected for official publication)</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.ago.state.co.us/press_detail.cfm?pressID=503 | title=Attorney General Announces Sentence | date=2001-03-16 | access-date=2007-09-29 | publisher=Colorado Department of Law | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060929012047/http://www.ago.state.co.us/press_detail.cfm?pressID=503 | archive-date=2006-09-29 | url-status=dead }}</ref>
